# Rationalistic Criticisms
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: What I have said of the theory of truth will, I am sure, have appeared obscure and unsatisfactory to most of you by reason of us brevity.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: I shall make amends for that hereafter.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: In a lecture on 'common sense' I shall try to show what I mean by truths grown petrified by antiquity.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: In another lecture I shall expatiate on the idea that our thoughts become true in proportion as they successfully exert their go-between function.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: In a third I shall show how hard it is to discriminate subjective from objective factors in Truth's development.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: You may not follow me wholly in these lectures; and if you do, you may not wholly agree with me.
  ¶1 UNCOVERED: But you will, I know, regard me at least as serious, and treat my effort with respectful consideration.
  ¶2 PARTIAL (uncovered in CAPS): YOU WILL PROBABLY BE SURPRISED TO LEARN, THEN, THAT Messrs.
  ¶2 UNCOVERED: In influential quarters Mr. Schiller, in particular, has been treated like an impudent schoolboy who deserves a spanking.
  ¶2 PARTIAL (uncovered in CAPS): I SHOULD NOT MENTION THIS, BUT FOR THE FACT THAT IT throws so much sidelight upon that rationalistic temper to which I have opposed the temper of pragmatism.
  ¶3 UNCOVERED: See the exquisite contrast of the types of mind!
  ¶3 UNCOVERED: If the two universes were offered, he would always choose the skinny outline rather than the rich thicket of reality.
  ¶3 UNCOVERED: It is so much purer, clearer, nobler.
  ¶4 UNCOVERED: I hope that as these lectures go on, the concreteness and closeness to facts of the pragmatism which they advocate may be what approves itself to you as its most satisfactory peculiarity.
  ¶4 PARTIAL (uncovered in CAPS): IT only follows HERE the example of the sister-sciences, interpreting the unobserved by the observed.
  ¶4 PARTIAL (uncovered in CAPS): It converts the absolutely empty notion of a static relation of 'correspondence' (WHAT THAT MAY MEAN WE MUST ASK LATER) between our minds and reality, into that of a rich and active commerce (that anyone may follow in detail and understand) between particular thoughts of ours, and the great universe of other experiences in which they play their parts and have their uses.
